claims.text: Net degradation of high-entropy alloys under tribo-corrosion is governed by a dynamic equilibrium between mechanical removal of a passive oxide and its repassivation.
The coupled wear-corrosion response results from competition between film disruption during sliding and chemical recovery of the film.
The initial high-entropy alloy is homogeneous.
The alloy naturally forms a thin protective oxide film under ambient conditions.
The self-forming passive oxide film is the structural mediator of the tribo-corrosion response.
Sliding mechanically disrupts the passive film.
Disruption of the passive film exposes fresh metal to the corrosive medium.
Freshly exposed metal undergoes repassivation in the corrosive medium.
Net degradation is determined by the relative rates of film removal and film reformation.
Degradation accelerates when mechanical film removal outpaces repassivation.
Tribo-corrosion degradation will exceed the sum of degradation measured under wear-only and corrosion-only conditions.
Increasing sliding speed or load removes the protective film more rapidly.
Increasing sliding speed or load raises the corrosion rate relative to the matched baselines.
Increasing sliding speed or load increases wear-induced material loss relative to the matched baselines.
The prediction should hold where a passive film can continuously reform under moderate conditions.
The prediction may fail in sufficiently aggressive environments that prevent passive-film formation.
The prediction may fail when a mechanically robust film forms and resists removal by sliding.
Extreme temperatures may invalidate the prediction by altering passivation kinetics.
Film-removal and repassivation kinetics may vary with small changes in alloy composition.
